verdict.summary: To read and send customers' Gmail you must register your own Google OAuth app, and Gmail read/send scopes are restricted. That means Google verification and an annual third-party security assessment if you store the data on servers. Credentials are quick to get; production approval is the long part.
verdict.biggestLaunchRisk: Restricted-scope verification plus the annual third-party security assessment: Google says verification can take several months, and one community post reports almost 3 months. Until it is done, your app is capped at 100 new users.

specialRequirements: verified domain / authorized domain with publicly accessible app homepage
annual third-party security assessment (if restricted scope data is stored or transmitted on servers)

managedCovers.text: Composio's directory lists Gmail under Composio-managed OAuth apps, so a shared managed OAuth app is available as an alternative to registering your own.
Whether managed OAuth is enough for prototyping an agent against test Gmail accounts is not detailed in the sources; Composio's directory only supports the managed-status statement.

youNeedOwnWhen.text: You want your own brand (app name, logo, privacy policy and terms links) on the Google consent screen. That is configured on your own project and subject to brand verification.
You launch to external users with restricted Gmail scopes and store or transmit that data on servers: the verification and security assessment attach to your own production project.
Whether a managed shared app can satisfy Google's restricted-scope requirements for your use case is not answered by the provided sources.

requirements.text: A Google Cloud project, and registering your app with Google Auth before you can create an OAuth client.
Gmail API enabled in the API Library before its scopes can be added to the consent screen.
External user type: the app starts in testing mode, available only to listed test users.
A separate production Google Cloud project; Google's OAuth policies require separate projects for testing and production.
A website on a verified domain with publicly accessible app and privacy policy information.
Consent screen details: app name, optional logo, support email, privacy policy and terms of service links.
Scopes justification and a contact email in the verification submission.
Verification for sensitive or restricted scopes unless an exception applies (personal use, internal use, development/testing).
Annual security assessment by a Google-approved third party if you access restricted data from or through a third-party server.
Production OAuth clients must not contain test redirect URIs or JavaScript origins available only to your team.
A registered legal business entity is not stated as required in the sources.

steps.title: Sign in and create or select a Google Cloud project
steps.detail: Sign in with a Google account and create a Google Cloud project for development. Your app needs a project to access Google OAuth APIs.
steps.agentPrep: List who should be project owners/editors so Google can reach the right contacts.

steps.title: Enable the Gmail API
steps.detail: Open the API Library, find Gmail API and click Enable. If prompted, enable billing and accept the API's Terms of Service. This must happen before Gmail scopes can be added.

steps.title: Register the app and configure the consent screen (External)
steps.detail: Register the app with Google Auth and set user type to External. Add app name, support email, optional logo, and privacy policy and terms links. The app starts in testing mode with listed test users.
steps.agentPrep: Draft app name, description, support email text, privacy policy and terms content.

steps.title: Create the OAuth client and store the secret
steps.detail: On the Google Auth Platform Clients page, click Create Client, choose the application type (a web application for a server-side agent) and create it. The client secret is shown only once, so store it securely.

steps.title: Build and test with listed test users
steps.detail: Implement the OAuth flow requesting only the narrowest Gmail scopes needed to read and send. Use the testing project with test users. Request scopes in code that exactly match those on the consent screen.
steps.agentPrep: Map each agent feature (read, send) to the minimum Gmail scope.

steps.title: Prepare a verified domain, public homepage and privacy policy
steps.detail: Verification needs a website on a verified domain with publicly accessible app and privacy policy information, and the domain listed as an authorized domain.
steps.agentPrep: Draft the homepage copy and privacy policy, including how restricted Gmail data is stored and used.

steps.title: Create and configure a separate production project
steps.detail: Create a separate production Google Cloud project with its own OAuth client, with no test-only redirect URIs or origins. Repeat the API enablement and consent screen configuration there, and select all Gmail scopes you use.

steps.title: Submit brand verification
steps.estimate: Minutes automated; manual review 2-3 business days
steps.detail: Click Verify Branding for the production app. Automated checks usually take minutes; if no automatic result, manual review usually takes 2-3 business days.

steps.title: Submit the app for restricted-scope verification
steps.detail: On the consent screen page click Submit for verification. Add the scopes justification, a contact email and any other helpful information, then submit.
steps.agentPrep: Draft the justification for each Gmail scope and the explanation of server-side data handling.

steps.title: Wait for Google's verification review
steps.estimate: Several months per Google; no firm range
steps.detail: Google says verification can take several months depending on data sensitivity; one community post reports almost 3 months. You can keep building and testing meanwhile. Until verified, the unverified app screen shows and new users are capped at 100.

steps.title: Complete the third-party security assessment
steps.detail: If you store or transmit restricted-scope data on servers, a Google-approved third party must perform a security assessment, and it recurs annually. Cost and duration are not stated in the sources.
steps.agentPrep: Gather architecture, data-storage and security-control documentation for the assessor.

steps.title: Publish and confirm scopes match
steps.detail: After approval, confirm the scopes requested in code match the consent screen exactly. Otherwise users still see the unverified app screen.

scopesAndNuances.text: Apps requesting sensitive or restricted scopes must complete verification unless an exception applies (personal use, development/testing, internal use, and others).
Restricted-scope apps must meet additional requirements and submit to extra reviews, which include a possible security assessment.
Apps accessing restricted data from or through a third-party server must undergo an annual security assessment by a Google-approved third party.
Unverified apps using sensitive/restricted scopes show an unverified app screen and are limited to 100 new users until verified.
Request the narrowest scopes needed; this is a stated requirement.
Brand verification applies to External, published apps that show a logo or display name on the consent screen.
The Setting up OAuth 2.0 help page is marked as no longer up to date; Google points to the Manage OAuth Clients article instead.
Exactly which Gmail scopes are restricted versus sensitive is not listed in the provided text; Google points to its OAuth verification FAQ for the current list.

blockers.problem: Verification is pending or incomplete, so users see an unverified app screen and new users are capped at 100.
blockers.fix: Submit the production project for verification with scopes justification, keep the scopes in code identical to the consent screen, and plan for a long wait.
blockers.contact: Google OAuth verification team via the verification submission

blockers.problem: Verification takes months; a community post reports almost 3 months of waiting for Gmail API approval.
blockers.fix: Submit early and keep building and testing in the meantime. Avoid launch dates that depend on approval.

blockers.problem: Server-side storage of restricted Gmail data triggers an annual third-party security assessment.
blockers.fix: Plan for the assessment early with a Google-approved assessor. Minimizing stored data may reduce scope, but the sources do not say it removes the requirement.

blockers.problem: Domain or privacy policy fails verification: no verified domain or publicly accessible app and privacy policy information.
blockers.fix: Host a public homepage and privacy policy on a verified, authorized domain before submitting.
